Precision Oxygen Therapeutics

BHOC - Biological Hemoglobin Oxygen Carrier

For immediate, controlled microvascular and tissue-level oxygenation while endogenous erythropoiesis recovers.

A donor-independent oxygen carrier with long shelf life at room temperature, designed to be endotoxin-free and red-cell-antigen-free, with compatibility across all blood types. For all species.

Development objectives. Species-specific dosing, safety and efficacy require independent evidence.

The Science Bridge

Every species is different.
The need for oxygen is universal.

BHOC Therapeutics is developing a next-generation oxygen carrier designed to support veterinary medicine, including wildlife, exotic and endangered species. By improving oxygen delivery at the microcirculatory level, we aim to help more animals survive when every second counts.

Discover the Science
  • Compatible with all blood types for all species.
  • 3+ year shelf life at room temperature.

Advancing oxygen delivery for a wilder tomorrow.

Biodiversity context

Catalogue of Life global Animalia species catalogue 1,780,634described animal species
IUCN Red List of Threatened Species global assessment databaseMore than175,900species assessed
IUCN Red List 2026-1 threatened species updateMore than49,500threatened with extinction

How many species? How many blood-group systems?

Different blood. One shared need: oxygen.

BHOC is being developed as one donor-independent oxygen-delivery platform with potential across species, compatibility across blood types, long room-temperature shelf life and reduced reliance on blood-bank logistics.

Development goal. Evidence remains product- and species-specific.

Related chemistry. Different roles.

Heme and chlorophyll belong to the tetrapyrrole family. Their metals, ring structures and side chains differ.

Hemoglobin transports oxygen. Chlorophyll absorbs light in photosynthesis.

BHOC Veterinary Therapeutics, also known as BHOC Vet, is led by Archil Jaliashvili. The BHOC Species & Biodiversity Protection Initiative connects oxygen delivery science with the future of animal health and species protection.

Our foundation is comparative biology: different species have different blood group systems, yet most vertebrates share hemoglobin-based oxygen transport. We explore how this foundation can inform species-specific research and development.
